reading.body:
Retail AI is tracked by four independent sources covering adoption, store technology, market size, and software spend, but none of them measures the compute or power behind those systems.

The four sources form a layered measurement stack. Census BTOS updates adoption every two weeks across all sectors, including retail trade. NRF adds detail on store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight sizes the market for merchandising and supply-chain logistics, while IHL tracks software expenditure and operational return in grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. Adoption is measured rather than guessed, and the Census series updates often enough to show change.

For AI specifically, the volume use cases are demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation. These run across many stores and transactions, so even small changes in adoption or software spend can signal where inference workloads are growing. But the data stops at adoption and spend. None of the four sources reports electricity demand, data center capacity, or compute requirements, so the data cannot support claims about grid constraints or building needs for retail AI.

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
Retail AI adoption is measured rather than estimated. According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 16.8% of retail trade firms (NAICS 44-45) answered yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks, up from 16.5% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023 and is updated fortnightly, which makes retail one of the sectors where the official number moves on a regular schedule.

The trade body coverage points to where that use sits. The National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software, and its research is described here as where retail AI adoption gets counted. The conversations the NRF reports from Paris centered on practical AI, connected stores, and relationship-driven loyalty, which places the emphasis on store operations and customer relationships rather than back-office experiments.

The research firms in this sector concentrate on merchandising and supply chain. Coresight produces adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics, and runs an invite-only forum on AI for consumer-focused businesses. IHL Group tracks retail technology expenditure and operational return across grocery, apparel, and general merchandise, and its published work includes a 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, in cooperation with Chain Store Age, finding that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards. IHL also reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, and frames the problem as what stalls AI pilots before they reach the store floor.

The money and the deployments cluster around inventory and fulfillment. IHL puts inventory distortion at $1.7 trillion, with empty shelves still costing $690.9 billion, and notes that AI agents no longer wait. On the platform side, Amazon asked Meta to remove its e-commerce site from Muse, Meta's AI shopping agent, saying it did not authorize the tool's access, while Amazon's own AI-backed Buy for Me tool enables purchases from external sellers. Amazon is also expanding smart-glasses trials for delivery drivers using computer vision, AI, cameras, and precision geospatial technology, after 275,000 test deliveries, with plans for 5,000 additional devices and a target of 20,000 deployed by the end of 2027. Castle Resorts and Hotels used AI-assisted development to launch a unified direct-booking wrapper across 20 properties, connecting five reservation systems and giving the operator in-house control for rapid testing and promotions.

The sources here do not report ROI figures for retail AI beyond IHL's operational return framing and its finding on inventory data accuracy, and they do not describe a regulatory posture for the sector. What a reader deciding whether to deploy should take from the material is narrower: the official adoption rate is modest and measured, the documented value sits in inventory visibility and accuracy rather than budget size, and the reported failure mode is spending on the wrong layer before pilots reach the store floor.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research describes itself as delivering data-driven insights on retail and technology, and claims a depth of expertise in China that it calls "unique in the industry." Its page also promotes a Shoptalk Fall 2026 Day 3 morning line-up, listing sessions on David's Bridal and Equinox selling past the core product, Crocs and Kenneth Cole marketing through entertainment, and Claire's and The Children's Place checking AI against the store. Coresight adds that it leads an invite-only yet collaborative forum exploring AI and the opportunities and challenges it presents for consumer-focused businesses.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
